subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Anatomy of a Wildfire
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Anatomy of a Wildfire.

hook.text: A wildfire needs three things: heat, fuel, and oxygen. Remove one and the fire dies.

buildup.text: Dry vegetation acts as fuel. A single lightning strike or discarded cigarette can ignite it.

discovery.text: Wind feeds oxygen to the flames and carries embers kilometers ahead, starting new fires.

twist.text: Crown fires leap from treetop to treetop at speeds that outrun firefighters on foot.

climax.text: Large fires create their own weather — generating thunderstorms and fire tornadoes.

punchline.text: A wildfire doesn't just burn in the weather. It becomes the weather.

quiz.question: What three elements does a wildfire need to burn?

details.summary: A wildfire needs fuel, heat, and oxygen — the fire triangle — and spreads through radiation, convection, and direct flame contact. Large wildfires generate their own weather, creating winds, pyrocumulus clouds, and even fire tornadoes that accelerate spread.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding fire behavior is essential for firefighter safety and community protection. Climate change is creating fire conditions that exceed historical experience.
takeaways: Fuel, heat, and oxygen comprise the fire triangle
Large fires create their own wind systems and weather
Fire spreads fastest uphill and with the wind

faq.question: How do wildfires create their own weather?
faq.answer: Intense heat generates powerful updrafts that pull in surrounding air, creating strong surface winds feeding the fire. Hot air rises to form pyrocumulus clouds that can produce lightning and create erratic, dangerous winds including fire tornadoes.

faq.question: What is an ember attack?
faq.answer: Burning embers carried by wind can ignite new fires kilometers ahead of the main front. This spotting behavior is the primary way wildfires jump firebreaks, roads, and rivers, making them extremely difficult to contain during high winds.
